title: How To Get Students To Raise Their Hand https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/02/13/how-to-get-your-students-to-raise-their-hand/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin makes the case for strictly requiring hand-raising, arguing that calling out kills lesson momentum, is unfair to less assertive students, inhibits independent thinking time, gives socially confident students an unfair advantage, and encourages rude, selfish classroom behavior. He then offers a six-step method for teaching the procedure: model exactly how to raise a hand correctly, demonstrate the 'how not to' version of common violations, have students practice with low-stakes questions, explicitly limit or close discussion during times requiring focus, ignore students who call out or wave their hands, and enforce the rule with a consequence when necessary. He notes one exception for small-group settings like guided reading, where freer conversation is appropriate, and closes by affirming that consistent enforcement of hand-raising is achievable and essential to effective teaching.
points: Calling out kills lesson momentum, is unfair to less assertive students, and interferes with independent thinking time.
Teaching hand-raising involves six steps: model correctly, show the 'how not to' version, practice, limit discussion times, ignore call-outs, and enforce with a consequence.
Explicitly closing the room for discussion at certain times (e.g., before independent reading) helps students understand when hand-raising is required.
Ignore students who call out or wave their hands rather than accidentally rewarding the behavior with a response.
The only exception to strict hand-raising is small-group settings like guided reading or literature circles, which allow freer conversation.
quotes: Calling out is a momentum killer of the highest order and can turn a well-planned lesson into a halting mess.
Every student has a right to participate, not just those who are more assertive. If calling out is allowed, a segment of your classroom will rarely be heard from.
Students who participate do better than those who don’t. Allowing students to call out gives socially confident students an unfair advantage.
Your students need to know exactly what you expect from them. The most effective way to do this is to sit in a student’s chair, and show them precisely how you want them to raise their hand.
Show your students how not to raise their hand. Act out common unacceptable behaviors.
If a student calls out and waves their hand at you, first ignore them. Send the message that you don’t respond to anything except proper hand raising.
I’ve never known a teacher who was lax in this area and didn’t have problems with student behavior, learning, engagement, time management, and more.
